reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: A benign but locally aggressive and highly vascular tumour occurring almost exclusively in adolescent males
The classic presentation is progressive unilateral nasal obstruction with recurrent, sometimes profuse, spontaneous epistaxis
It is thought to arise near the sphenopalatine foramen and spreads submucosally into the nasopharynx, nasal cavity, pterygopalatine fossa, and potentially the orbit and intracranial compartment
Examination reveals a firm reddish mass in the nasopharynx or nasal cavity, and a mass in an adolescent male should raise strong suspicion of angiofibroma
Contrast-enhanced imaging shows an intensely enhancing mass, often with anterior bowing of the posterior maxillary wall (Holman-Miller sign), and defines intracranial or orbital extension
Biopsy is generally avoided because of the serious bleeding risk, and diagnosis rests largely on the characteristic clinical and imaging picture
Preoperative angiography with embolisation of feeding vessels reduces intraoperative haemorrhage
Surgical excision, endoscopic or open depending on extent, is the mainstay, with radiotherapy reserved for extensive or unresectable intracranial disease
reference.pathophysiology: Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a histologically benign tumour composed of a fibrous stroma interspersed with numerous thin-walled vascular channels that frequently lack a complete muscular coat, which explains the tendency to torrential bleeding. It typically originates around the sphenopalatine foramen and pterygopalatine fossa and grows submucosally along natural pathways, expanding into the nasopharynx and nasal cavity and eroding bone to reach the orbit, infratemporal fossa, and skull base. Its almost exclusive occurrence in adolescent males has prompted the hypothesis of hormonal (androgen) sensitivity influencing growth.
additionalDifferentials: Encephalocoele presenting as a nasopharyngeal mass
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging to define the tumour extent, bony erosion, and intracranial or orbital spread
Angiography to identify feeding vessels (commonly branches of the internal maxillary artery) and enable preoperative embolisation
Nasal endoscopy to assess the mass while avoiding biopsy
Full blood count and cross-matching in anticipation of significant blood loss
redFlags: Recurrent or profuse epistaxis that can be life-threatening from this highly vascular tumour
Biopsy in the clinic setting risking uncontrolled haemorrhage and generally to be avoided
Intracranial or orbital extension threatening vision or neurological structures
Rapid enlargement or cranial nerve involvement requiring urgent specialist management
reference.prognosis: Although histologically benign, the tumour is locally aggressive and prone to recurrence when incompletely excised; complete removal, aided by preoperative embolisation, gives good long-term control, while extensive skull-base or intracranial disease is more difficult to eradicate and may require radiotherapy.
pitfalls: Performing an outpatient biopsy of a vascular nasopharyngeal mass and precipitating severe bleeding
Dismissing recurrent epistaxis in an adolescent male as trivial
Underestimating tumour extent by omitting cross-sectional imaging and angiography
Inadequate resection leaving residual tumour at the skull base with subsequent recurrence
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
